passage:
Layla ran the student food-bank drive in Lyon, answered every friend's 2 a.m. messages, and cried at the end of films she had seen five times. This week she had sorted four hundred tins, stayed up with Olga after a break-up, and argued with her flatmate about the dishes at midnight.
On Thursday she sat on the kitchen floor, too tired to open the fridge.
Olga found her there. 'You carry everyone. Who carries you?'
Layla laughed, then cried. 'I don't know how to care less.'
'Don't care less. Care on a schedule.' They made a list together: dinner at seven, no matter what. Phone off at midnight. The dishes talk would wait till Sunday morning, when she wasn't exhausted.
On Sunday the talk took ten calm minutes.

qa.q: How many tins had Layla sorted this week?
qa.a: Four hundred tins.

qa.q: What does Layla sitting on the kitchen floor, too tired to open the fridge, show?
qa.a: It shows she was overwhelmed and exhausted from giving so much to everyone at once.

qa.q: Which choice about the dishes talk made it go better?
qa.a: Waiting till Sunday morning, when she wasn't exhausted, turned a midnight argument into ten calm minutes.

qa.q: How does Olga see Layla's way of caring?
qa.a: Olga values how much Layla carries but worries that nobody carries her, so Olga suggests caring on a schedule rather than caring less.

grounding: Shows a young adult who gives everything to friends and causes and gets exhausted, then learns routines and better timing for hard talks.

passage:
In the college theatre club's green room, Trisha had been the first to arrive and the last to leave for three weeks. She painted sets, rewrote scenes at 3 a.m., and still took every late call from her roommate, who was going through a rough patch. On the night of the dress rehearsal she forgot her own lines twice and burst into tears in the wings.
Manoj, the final-year student directing the play, sat on an upturned crate beside her. 'Your fire is why this play works,' he said. 'But you can't pour it all out every day and expect any left.'
She wiped her face. 'I don't know how to do half.'
'Not half. Rhythm. Sleep by one. One day off a week. And tell your roommate you'll talk at lunch, not at three in the morning.'
Trisha nodded slowly.

qa.q: When did Trisha rewrite scenes?
qa.a: At 3 a.m.

qa.q: What made Trisha burst into tears in the wings?
qa.a: Exhaustion from giving everything to the play and to her roommate caught up with her, and forgetting her lines twice tipped her over.

qa.q: What choice does Manoj ask Trisha to make, and why?
qa.a: To keep a rhythm: sleep by one, a day off each week, and roommate talks at lunch, so her depth of feeling doesn't drain her completely.

qa.q: How might Trisha's roommate feel about talking at lunch instead of at 3 a.m.?
qa.a: The roommate may feel a little let down at first but may also get a more rested, attentive Trisha.

grounding: Shows a young adult pouring herself into a passion and a roommate's troubles until she is overwhelmed, and learning rhythm and timing to keep going.

My brother Ojas has a friend, Kashish, who calls him whenever things go wrong. Last Sunday Kashish came over, eyes swollen, and asked to stay with us 'for a few months' after a fight with his landlord.

Harsha, you think I was always this old man who cries at films? At fifteen I was told, 'Men don't cry, Yusuf.' When my elder brother left for work in the Gulf and I didn't know when I'd see him again, I went behind the well and bit my sleeve so no one would hear.

Sunday night, hostel
Went home to the village for Eid. Within an hour I was back to a soft voice, head down, 'ji Abbu', speaking only our dialect. I touched Dadi's feet, ate with my hands and sat quietly while the uncles talked.
Back in the city tonight, Anand asked how the trip was, and I answered in fast English, cracked jokes, called him bro. He laughed and said, 'Wasim, you're two different people.'
It stung. Am I fake in one of those places?
I thought about it on the balcony. At home, being quiet is how I show respect. Here, speaking up is how I show I belong. The core is the same: I care about the people in front of me, and I don't lie to either side.
Maybe that's not two people. Maybe that's just knowing two languages of respect.

qa.q: What did Anand say that stung?
qa.a: 'Wasim, you're two different people.'

qa.q: What was Wasim worried about after Anand's comment?
qa.a: Wasim worried about being fake in one of the two places.

qa.q: What turning point helped Wasim make peace with switching styles?
qa.a: Thinking it over on the balcony, Wasim saw that quietness at home and speaking up in the city are both ways of showing respect, with the same honest core.

qa.q: How might Anand see Wasim if he visited the village?
qa.a: Anand might be surprised by the quiet, respectful Wasim, but could come to see the same caring person in a different setting.

grounding: Shows a young person moving between village and city who shifts language and boldness, feels split, and finds the honest core is the same.
